explain.say: Waves carry huge energy, especially in storms. When they crash against a cliff, they force water and air into cracks at enormous pressure, prising rock apart. This is hydraulic action.

faq.a: Hydraulic action is when waves smash into a cliff and squeeze water and air into cracks. The pressure, and the sudden release as the wave pulls back, widens the cracks and breaks off rock.
Abrasion is when waves throw sand, pebbles and boulders against the cliff, grinding and chipping it away like sandpaper.

faq.q: Why do some cliffs erode faster than others?
faq.a: Soft rock like clay erodes fast, sometimes metres a year, while hard rock like granite may wear back only millimetres. Big storms, exposed coasts and cracked rock also speed things up.
As a cliff retreats, it leaves behind a flat, rocky shelf at its old base, visible at low tide. This is a wave-cut platform.
asks: What is left when a cliff retreats?

faq.q: Can we stop cliffs from eroding?
faq.a: People slow it with sea walls, rock barriers and groynes, but these are costly and can increase erosion further along the coast. Sometimes it is better to let the coast move.

facts: Parts of the Holderness coast in England, made of soft clay, retreat by about 2 metres a year on average.
Waves in storms can exert pressures of many tonnes per square metre on cliffs.
